utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is Mr. Ivetic going to be joining us at some stage today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's working on that issue. He's in -- contacting our office this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if he's got one eye on what's happening here, something can perhaps be relayed to him. We are where we are on this issue of translation, and we need to address the whole thing as a matter of urgency, but it's clear that the first thing that needs to be done is to be absolutely sure what are the first 200 pages that require translation so that that job can be started today. Now, I've asked Mr. Dawson to take whatever steps he can to liaise between Mr. Ivetic and CLSS to get that bit done, never mind the rest, never mind the rights and wrongs of what's happened in the past. We'll address that as and when we're required to address it. But there are plainly schemes set up to enable translation to be done for you that are not being triggered and that need to be triggered today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, hopefully his time can be usefully spent today in making available or making it clear and removing any doubt about what the first 200 are. All right? Now, I will instruct Mr. Dawson to communicate with him by e-mail merely to set up a meeting about this among the three of them - that's CLSS, Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Dawson - there will be no other e-mail exchanges at this stage. I gather there have been several. I've seen -- I saw the one the other day about the numbers of documents, for example. I don't know the whole story. But there's no point in that continuing. Face-to-face meetings are the only way to resolve this at this stage, and hopefully by later today sometime that first step -- first hurdle will have been negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we left off yesterday, we were talking about Bela Crkva and where the general passed through. I discovered last night some additional aerial surveillance -- aerial photographs which show what I believe is the main road. This is shown in Exhibit P0093, which was not something I disclosed to the Defence. I sent an e-mail to Mr. Cepic and the rest of the Defence last night indicating that I would request this morning to be able to show that to the general because I think it would be a matter of interest to the Court and it may -- it may clear up where he passed through and where that was vis-a-vis the mosque, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then, General, if we could start off by showing you an exhibit, it's P0093. And I believe we need to go to page 8. Yes. General, do you recognise what's depicted there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the road leading towards Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could take the pen there perhaps and draw where that road is, and we'll mark this as an IC exhibit.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the road you told us about yesterday on which you drove by on the 4th of April and those other occasions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the mosque appears to be located in about the centre of this picture, slightly to the right of centre? Can you see it there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I had the advantage of sitting at my computer and using my magnifying tool on the computer. It appears that there is no minaret on the mosque at this time, and I would tell you this photograph was taken, I think, in late June 1999. Do you have any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason. But we would know -- we should know exactly when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is indicated at page 1 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But has that document -- or this photograph being exhibited already?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This entire exhibit, Your Honour, I think, was admitted on the 27th of September. This was part of the forensic package concerning Bela Crkva. That's all the questions I have on that, unless Your Honours have a question. Can we give this an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm just -- I'm trying to wrap up several loose ends I have and hope to finish before this session is over. So if you'll bear with me, I may flip from topic to topic. First of all, I wanted to ask you about radio call signs. During 1998 and 1999, did -- did you or any of your subordinate units use a radio call sign -- the word was "Koritnik," K-o-r-i-t-n-i-k. I'm not sure I'm pronouncing it correctly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koritnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that a call sign used by your units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My call sign was "Poljanica" usually. And my commanding officers had the same call sign, but each of us had a separate number; although, the name "Koritnik" is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did any of your battle groups use that call sign in either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was always "Poljanica." But it's possible that this sign "Koritnik" was related to call signs of Prizren in communication with Pristina, but I'm not sure. It's not necessarily Prizren. It could be some other town. The call sign is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say a call sign of -- of Prizren, who do you mean? What -- is that a military body in --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prizren garrison, the Prizren -- the Prizren garrison, the Djakovica garrison, Pristina garrison. Everybody had a call sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about the call sign "Pastrik"? Does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who that pertained to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been one of the units. Maybe the Buza [phoen] Battalion. If you have a document, that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me show you Exhibit P1052. There are three separate pages here. Let's have a look and see if you can help us with any of those. And, actually, the first page doesn't have any units related to the 549th, but we see a reference to battle group of the 125th being "Ibar". Did you ever hear that call sign in connection with the 125th or any of their subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear it's connected to the 125th here, but all names, all place names were used in various communication plans, so I heard all these names, "Pastrik" and "Ibar," but -- I can see this, but it has nothing to do with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 of the B/C/S, which I think pertains to the English page that's up right now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this one, General, you'll see number 5 is listed as "1 BG 549th" with the call sign "Koritnik-40". Does that refresh your recollection about whether any of your subordinate units may have used that call sign?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This call sign was used in interactions through communications, but in radio communications we used the normal call sign that I told you about, but "Koritnik-40" is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I'm not understanding what's the difference between radio communications and "interactions through communications," is how it was translated in your last answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is when you use stations, when you exchange telegrams, and this document specifies on which frequencies this is done. We had our normal call sign, "Poljanica," and it changed every ten days; that is, only numbers changed but the sign "Poljanica" remained for all commanders, but it was the number that told you which unit is which and which commander is which. I see that "Pastrik" -- "Pastrik" is familiar. That was Pristina. Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the third page, please. And here we do see the second item is the forward command post for the Pristina Corps with a call sign of "Pastrik-13".

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Pastrik" is the Pristina Corps in this communications at that time, because this should relate only to a specific period of time. You can also see that another one of my units is "Koritnik-80."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we have the wrong English page up for this one. We may have to get the first English page we put up this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if I understood your earlier answer, then, you said you might have used the term "Koritnik" in -- in communications -- in interactions through communications. I think you gave an example of -- like in a telegram. Are you saying then in a telegram there may have been a reference to some entity which was referred to by "Koritnik" with a number perhaps, so it's some sort of code name that is used in a telegram when you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment, General. One moment. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your view, I never heard "telegram" in the testimony of General Delic in relation to this issue, but if my learned friend kindly can suggest us, can give us the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's in -- in the English at page 6, line 20, where the translation of the answer is: "When you use stations, when you exchange telegrams, and this document specifies on which frequencies this is done." Was that part of your answer, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will return to Mr. Hannis' question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, is that correct, then? Are you saying this was not a call sign that would have been used on the radio but, rather, it was a sort of a code name that might be used in other communications, like telegrams?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koritnik was for a while assigned to my unit for a specific activity. And it was used towards the superior command. Towards subordinate units, we always used only "Poljanica."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what time period that was that "Koritnik" was used toward the superior commands?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. Probably sometime in 1998. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move on to another topic. You told us, I think, in your earlier testimony that -- that you -- you personally never saw any instances of identity documents being taken from the Kosovo Albanian refugees as they -- as they were leaving the country and going into Albania, but did you not testify in -- in Milosevic that you -- you did witness license plates being removed at the border from vehicles of those people leaving?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said such a thing. In my testimony at the Milosevic trial, I said that on one occasion - that was in the month of May - sometime in mid-May, perhaps the 15th of May, together with a foreign TV crew, Italian television, and perhaps another TV crew, from Denmark perhaps, that were in my area, including Daniel Schiffer, I was on the border and I saw license plates just thrown on the ground next to the customs building. I was surprised, so I came to see the chief of the secretariat to ask him whether he was aware of that, whether something like that had been ordered. He, too, was surprised and he reacted immediately, to the effect that something like that was not allowed. Otherwise, I had no need to go to the border crossing. I only came because of those TV reporters who wanted to cross over to the other side and contact with other reporters who were in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. General, I was referring to your testimony on the 6th of July, 2005 at page 41946, which in the exhibit we have here, it's page 1162. And I -- your direct answer was: "I noticed that the border, there were quite a few registration plates that were taken off. That's what I noticed primarily. I didn't see the documents." But are you talking about -- are you talking about ten license plates or are you talking about hundreds? I had the impression that it was a significant number enough for you to go make inquiries about it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot, several dozen license plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, mid-May. It could have very well been the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Could we now look at Exhibit P1425. General, this is a -- a report from you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just one moment. Could you say again, Mr. Delic, how many license plates you saw, in rough terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said, "several dozen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I want to show you Exhibit P1425. As I was saying, this is dated the 8th of August, 1998 and a report from you on how your units were engaged in combat task for the period 18 July to 6 of August. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy is rather poor. Could we zoom in. Yes, this could be a document from my brigade. If we could see the signature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If we could go to the bottom of the page. And I guess on to the next page, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you need that enlarged?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. You should just enhance the passage you want to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in this document you're reporting about having engaged in activities with the MUP in various locations, including Bela Crkva, Orahovac in -- on the 18th and 19th of July, as well as other locations. On this page we have a, at the bottom you're talking about some of the problems, and one of them is that -- that it appears that the MUP sometimes expected the army to carry out the entire task. And you're indicating that the role of the VJ was to provide support. Is that a problem that you experienced in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here relates to one problem that occurred on the 25th of July, 1998, when one unit of the MUP from Pirot refused to set out and carry out a task. And in the course of execution of that task, another unit - I believe from Leskovac - also stopped dead in its tracks and this task could not be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After this, did you continue to have similar problems in joint operations, or did you work that out and not experience the problem again after the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerned one activity, from the 25th until perhaps the 27th of July, during one combat action. Because for those MUP units, it was their first combat action as well, and that's probably the reason why this problem occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I want to ask you about some of the war diaries of your subordinate units. Are you aware, first of all, that-- that subordinate units - for example, the 2nd Battalion, the Armoured Battalion - kept their own war diaries?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the duty of every unit at the level of battalion to keep a war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to review or -- or see any of those war diaries before testifying here this year?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 2005 I saw the war diary of the 2nd Battalion. I did not look at other war diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In looking at that war diary, did you see anything in it that was not consistent with your knowledge of what had transpired during the war? Did you see anything there that you believed or knew was wrong or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read these diaries in detail. I only looked at entries for certain dates I was interested in, and I didn't find anything there out of the ordinary, nothing special. They were written in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if you recall whether the 2nd Battalion was engaged in a task of -- of blocking Korenica and a line that included Korenica and Meja or -- on or around the 26th and 27th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That battalion was defending the border, and with a part of its forces it was blocking one line, but it should be written in that diary. I believe it was Korenica, and then the next place, Madenaj, I don't know if Meja is mentioned. Because I received that sort of thing in reports from battalions. I know they were on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate that -- this diary is found at Exhibit P2019, and we'll make submissions on it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you, General, about the Armoured Battalion. If we could look at Exhibit P2574. First of all, can you tell me, who was -- who was the commander of the Armoured Battalion in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can see. That's a cover page. If we could go to the page 2 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English. I think you told me just a minute ago, General, that you had not seen this one before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the English page, which has the entry for the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm having trouble locating the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General, if you -- do you see the entry for the 25th of March? Could -- could you read that for me? Because on my notes, there's some questions about the translation that I had notes about. Are you able to read that, or do we need to enlarge it for you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can enlarge a little bit. Thank you. "At 6.45, the unit marched to the Landovica sector, and after carrying out reconnaissance, three tank platoons were set up, and in the evening hours they were sent to the sector of the village of Zrze." And it is impossible -- well, I is see that Major Nenad Stevanovic is mentioned and Second Lieutenant Medic Dragan and Dragan Skrbic and the last one was transferred to the Brnjaca sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was Major Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a battalion commander. Medic was one of the komandiri and so was Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could read a little farther on. We have in the English translation another reference to the commander of the 549th Chief of Staff. That may -- I'm not sure if that's on the bottom of this B/C/S page you have or if we have to go to the next page. See, there's a reference to elevation 451? Can you read from there, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Major Nenad Stevanovic with the 5th Company of the PJP and the liberation of the village of Brestovac along the axis Baksina-Baksina Strana-Brestovacke Padine, elevation 451, with the 2nd Tank Platoon and the PJP Company under the command of the Chief of Staff of the 549th Motorised Brigade. The attack went along the axis of the Orahovac and Brestovac village, and in the same village they spent the night after it was liberated."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could stop you there. It's been translated as your -- what you read was translated as the -- with the 2nd Tank Platoon and the PJ [sic] commander, the command of the Chief of Staff. It's not clear to me. Was the Chief of Staff commanding the PJP as well as the tank platoon, or how do you understand that entry?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff at that time was the commander of Combat Group 7. Combat Group 7, that was a combat group that was composed of my troops. Among those troops was the tank platoon. But he's just writing about the tank platoon. He's not writing about the other forces, forces from the other units. So these are the tank platoons that had arrived in the night of the 24th, and in the morning they joined those units, the Combat Groups 6, 7, and 2. Because otherwise, they were not part of their organic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Hannis, if that's really been helpful. Do you not think we should go over that again, that translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because it's -- it's not the same as what's on the document, the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I agree, Your Honour. It's -- the reason I asked the question was because the English translation here was not clear to me. I'm not sure that the answer I have now is any clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the English translation is very clear in the sense that it attributes command of the PJP to a VJ officer, but that's not what the answer that the witness has given says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, could you have a look at that again, because our English translation suggests that the -- that the PJP company in this particular action was commanded by the Chief of Staff of the 549th. Is that not what it says?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read once again. "With the 2nd Tank Platoon and the PJP company, which was under the command of the Chief of Staff of the 549th Motorised Brigade, which was attacking along the axis" -- regardless of what was written here, the Chief of Staff was commanding the Combat Group 7, and this is quite obvious from all the documents. This is a battalion diary, but this is what it says here in effect, really. And it is impossible for the Chief of Staff to command a company and a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I understand you say that all the documents show that and that it's not possible, but that is what it says in B/C/S, isn't it, that the -- that the -- or that the Chief of Staff is commanding the tank platoon and -- and the PJP company? That's what it says. Maybe it was written down wrong, but what is what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a misinterpretation. It says: "With the tank platoon" not "the tank battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I agree, and I think I said "tank platoon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may have been translated differently, though. But that's been helpful. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if now we could move to page 4 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S, one more entry in this diary I want to ask you about. It's on the 18th of April. Do you find that in your B/C/S? I think we'll have to enlarge the page on the bottom right. Yeah. That last one. Are you able to read that now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about the -- the last sentence. It says, in the English translation: "Sergeant -- Sergeant Igor Petlic intercepted refugees and appropriated 2.000 Deutschmarks." You were aware of that incident, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I heard about Sergeant Petrovic maybe. It's not really very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you -- you did more than hear about it, didn't you? Didn't you write a warning to your -- to your subordinates in which you made reference to this sergeant and this incident? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Sergeant Petrovic was mentioned in a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, our English has been translated as -- as "Petlic," but I think you're right that it was "Petrovic." If we could show you now Exhibit 5D895, which is dated two days later, the 20th of April. And this is -- this is from you. First of all, in the first paragraph, you say, starting at the end of the second line: "There have been individual cases of conduct in combat operations where the provisions and instructions regulating conduct in combat and the provisions of the International Law of War have not been applied in full." In addition to the incident with Sergeant Petrovic, what other individual cases did you have in mind or did you know about when you wrote this document? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you ask a lot of me. Of course I remember those cases, but you found Sergeant Petrovic in some kind of a diary and I had no knowledge that any such entry existed there. But as early as on the 20th he is mentioned in a warning, and it is noted here that he was arrested and sent to Nis to be criminally responsible, to be held criminally responsible. I responded to any case that came to my attention. My security organ, my police would respond the very same day. And it is noted here what he had done, and the commanding officers of units are warned about an order from the Pristina Corps, and then six or seven -- or rather, six tasks are listed here for the units. The commanding officers are warned hereby, because all those tasks and instructions had already been given to the units, so I don't see what's controversial about all this, because this shows that all the organs of the brigade carried out their tasks in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. You do mention Sergeant Petrovic in -- in paragraph 4 specifically, about being arrested, sent to Nis, held criminally liable for robbing a convoy of refugees. Now, in your reminder down below, you say: "Commands and specialised organs shall take effective measures to prevent all forms of crime, as has been ordered several times to date." How many times prior to the 20th of April had you given those kinds of warnings? When you say "several times," are you talking about five? Ten? Twenty?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a wrong interpretation. These are not special organs. This is command and professional organs, and by this we mean the military police organs. Every time when I noticed something happening in a unit, I would send out a warning specifying what had happened, and in many occasions I would even mention the name of the person involved. But one must stress the following: Every time I would receive a warning from my superior command - and on this occasion, that is warning 455-140 -- I -- 64 - I was supposed to relay that down to my units down the chain of command. Sometimes I would receive orders relating to the discipline. And if I received such an instruction from the Pristina Corps, I would have to do the same thing with this order I received from the corps commander, even though I may have written another order to that effect a couple of days earlier. So I would have to write my own order and send it to the lower units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, the same as yesterday, Mr. Hannis. You have to try to focus the witness on the particular point you're dealing with, which hasn't really been addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, General, when you got an order from your superior that you had to pass on those warnings. But in this case, this seems to be one that you generated yourself without a prior order, because you knew about the incident regarding Sergeant Petrovic. Isn't that part of the basis for you issuing this warning on this occasion? "Yes" or"no," if you can.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Hannis. If I may be allowed to explain. I received the warning with the number that is indicated here from the corps. But since I had had such a case in my own unit, I didn't have to pass on the warning from the Pristina Corps command. I did pass on those items, but the warning from the Pristina Corps also pertained to some events in other units, but that is not important for me. So I put that aside and I mentioned two cases that happened in my own unit, and that is why I referenced the warning from the Pristina Corps but I talk about incidentals in my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not issue warnings of your own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness had already said at 18.23: "Every time when I noticed something happening in a unit, I would send out a warning specifying what had happened, and on many occasions I would even mention the name of the person involved." Is that not the answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question, that I don't think you've answered yet, you said that this had been ordered several times to date. And I asked you if that meant, five, ten, twenty, or more. As of the 20th of April, how many previous times, approximately, had you issued such warnings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you insist, Mr. Hannis, at collegium meetings I sometimes issued verbal orders to my subordinate officers. This -- once they noted down in their notebooks, it becomes legally binding. I would have collegium meetings every other day in the evening. I would meet with my commanders. And they were always warned that they have to abide by the rules. I can say that I pointed them to that several dozen -- dozen times. I told them how important it was to stick by the rules, be it military discipline, International Law of War, or conduct in combat. At every meeting I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one of the reasons was because there were regular occurrences of crimes. That's why you had to keep reminding them; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not so. If you look at the number of people, there were less crimes than usual -- than what would be usual in peacetime. But even one crime, for me as an officer in a unit, is one crime too many. I wanted to have no crimes committed in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to Sergeant Petrovic and this -- this crime of robbing a convoy of refugees, in your exhibit, which is our P962, of the criminal proceedings against people in the 549th between May of 1998 and July of 1999, he's not listed. Do you know what happened to his case? Why isn't he listed in that report of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, as far as the unit is concerned, he went before the court and some measure was -- he was sanctioned, but I do know why he is not there on the list. When we asked from the military court to provide us with all the cases -- all the proceedings that have been instituted against the soldiers and officers in our unit, he was not on this list. And that is why I did not include him. But there is a criminal report against him, and he was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him? Wasn't he released in 2002, purportedly due to lack of evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I think that he was not released. I think that he was sentenced to a couple of months in prison. I don't know whether he actually served it or whether it was a suspended sentence, but I don't know that for a fact. I do know that he was brought before the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on. I'd like to show you Exhibit P -- or 5D878. This is from the 15th of February, 1999. General, do you recall this exhibit -- or this document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to direct you to a particular provision. And it's on the second page of the English, under item 3. And I think we may have to go to the second page of the B/C/S as well. Do you see the third paragraph under item 3 mentions that in January and February, most officers sent their families to Serbia and Montenegro. The last sentence in that paragraph says: "At the insistence of municipal administrative organs, we have again revised the 'Plan for the Protection of the Population in Case of an Armed Rebellion.'" Can you recall that? Was that something that you did?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated -- or rather, my officers participated in updating this plan. The plan had been in existence from an earlier time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that plan also include how the armed non-Siptar population was going to be engaged in protecting the population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This plan was quite simple. It's just a couple of pages. What it was all about is that there were villages where there were just a few houses, just a few Serbian households. And then, under the protection of the MUP primarily, they were to be moved into town. In this case, it was a sports hall, a gym of some sort, where they were to be accommodated and protected. And then furthermore, if the situation in the town got more serious, there were parts of the town where the Serbian population was in the minority, and then they were to be moved to those part of the -- parts of the town where they could be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this also dealt with providing assistance, medical assistance, food supplies, so there was no need for my units to get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. And -- and part of the way for reducing the need for units -- your units to be involved was to provide for task for the civilian protection, the civilian defence, and the armed non-Siptar population, that is, the Serb and Montenegrin population; correct? Weren't they included in this plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No mention is made of armed Serbian and Montenegrin population. As far as I can see, there is no mention of them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we don't have the plan in front of us. We just have this document referring to revising that plan. Let me now move to another exhibit related to that issue. Can we show you Exhibit P1976. And, General, I'll at -- tell you this is one of those Joint Command command orders. This is dated, I think, the 15th of April, 1999. And do you recall having received this order? It's for rounding and destroying the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Jezerce.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit played a less-important role.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that in a minute. If we could go to page 2 of the English. And on the B/C/S page, it's on the screen now. Could you look at item number 2, "Task of the Pristina Corps." And this has that phrase that we've seen several times before. It says: "The Pristina Corps with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population of Kosovo and Metohija supports the -- supports the MUP forces in routing and destroying of Siptar terrorists in the area of responsibility." Now, I want to follow up on that. If you could go down -- I'm not sure it's on this page for you. If it is, it's the last paragraph. And in English, it's near the bottom of page 2. The last sentence says: "Engage the armed non-Siptar population on safeguarding military facilities and communications and on the protection and defence of the non-Siptar population." So here we have a more specific task for the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. We don't see on our screens, or if it's possible in B/C/S, especially for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't it that -- I believe it was that last paragraph, at the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must have been on that page, Mr. Cepic, because the next page is paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe I made a mistake, but I didn't see it. Maybe it's my mistake, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see it, General? The last sentence on that page?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Yes, I can see it. It's the last sentence, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then do you know why that order specified that they be engaged in the protection and defence of the non-Siptar population, as opposed to all the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sentence that is quite illogical, and it is complete nonsense, what it says here. The armed non-Siptar population --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to stop you there, because you told us previously that these Joint Command orders were professionally and well written. The only problem was they had "Joint Command" in the title. Are you changing your mind now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not change my mind. But writing and mentioning the armed non-Siptar population -- and here you have tasks of the Pristina Corps. And if you go on to look at the tasks for the units, you see that the task is given to this armed non-Siptar population. A corps cannot issue any tasks to the armed non-Siptar population if it is under the defence -- or military departments and through them, with the Ministry of Defence, and they take care of that. They're in charge of them. So the army cannot command them. And in my zone, it would be particularly stupid, because I did not have any armed non-Siptar population in it, especially not the Serbs, because they had already been expelled from my zone, so I did not have any problems with that. But could you please look at the tasks of the unit so that I can see whether my unit was issued any tasks related to the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your -- your task is at 5.3, which is on page 5 of the English. And while we're looking for that, I -- I want to remind you, when we talked yesterday about your thesis, you -- and you talked about commanding the forces that would be used in dealing with the armed rebellion in Kosovo. You told us the problem was between the MUP and the VJ, because the law wasn't clear on how those competencies should be allocated, et cetera. But you said there was no problem regarding the civil protection, the civil defence, the armed non-Siptar population, because those bodies found the Ministry of Defence and because of the VJ's liaison with that, there wasn't a problem. And you told us in your thesis that the army had overall responsibility for the defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assertions are absolutely ridiculous, Mr. Hannis. Once again, you're talking about my final paper and not at a single point in time should that be allowed in this courtroom, to discuss that, because that is a school paper. In 2005 and today it is being discussed. My final paper is no official document. People will laugh in Belgrade when I tell them that this Court discussed my final paper for two hours. And the defence of that particular paper was half an hour in 1997. This is a pleasure for me or satisfaction that a court at this level discusses my final paper from university. But it is ridiculous to link that to what actually happened in 19--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you've made your point. Repeating it over and over does not add any strength to the point you've made. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, are you disowning your paper? I thought it was a pretty fine piece of work. It seems to describe pretty accurately what the situation was, and it foresaw pretty clearly what came to pass afterwards. Do you now want to remove yourself from it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are thinking along the wrong lines, Mr. Hannis. When I come back to Belgrade, I'm going to ask for my paper to be published, printed, publicised, but there is going to be a foreword too that will have to do with this Court. You told me about 5.3. As for my unit, there is no mention of armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but there is a task to ensure complete road passability and combat control over the territory, and one of the things that the armed non-Siptar population is supposed to do in that document is to ensure communications. Doesn't that relate to complete road passability? Do you need to go back and look at the tasks --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did you see a task for the armed non-Siptar population? You saw tasks for all units. But you only saw that task in general terms. There is not a single unit that involves a task for the armed non-Siptar population. It is perfectly reasonable for me within my zone to make sure that roads are accessible and that the territory is accessible, but not -- I'm not going to do that through the armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we -- we have a conundrum. We have the corps directed to engage - that's the word you used - the non-Siptar population and then no specific task given to them, and you say quite simply that that is illogical and complete nonsense. So that's where we stand on this. Can you help us to unravel it in some way? Just calm the emotions for a moment and tell us how we ought to see our way through what you say is the command of the VJ expressing themselves in an illogical and completely nonsensical way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2 of every order is the task received from the superior command. From paragraph 5 onwards are the tasks addressed to the subordinate units. It is obvious that the corps commander believed that the armed non-Siptar population has no role to play within this task. He issued tasks to all his units. I only see the task for my unit and part of the task for the 243rd Brigade, but nowhere is there any mention of the armed non-Siptar population within the brigades, and there is no mention of them in the tasks in specific terms as the armed non-Siptar population; therefore, they did not receive any tasks. As for me, I'm just carrying out paragraph 5.3, and nothing else in that order interests me, except from item 6 onwards and item 1, "Information about the enemy." It is only 5.3 that matters to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is there a specific task in any paragraph allocated to the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, there's not a specific enumerated task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Is one possibility, Mr. Delic, that should you find it necessary in executing your task to seek the assistance of the armed non-Siptar population, that you've got it from -- you've got authority for that from paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that was supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is that phrase "engage non-Siptar population" about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, you should know the level of organisation on the part of that population. In my zone, there practically weren't any people, because the previous population had been expelled the previous year and I had nothing and no one to organise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Address my question. What is that supposed to do in that document, that sentence, "engage the armed non-Siptar population"? Why is it there? -- Why is it there if there's no task? Or is that -- or is that what you say is illogical and nonsensical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm saying that it's illogical because it doesn't appear anywhere later in the tasks. There is no task for that population, and not a single commander could have used them. They get tasks through the Ministry of Defence through the Municipal Defence Department, and they have plans of their own and they carry out -- well, the civil defence and the civil protection, the population are tied to them, and they carry out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that, of course, depends on us accepting evidence that the armed non-Siptar population is a reference to civil defence and civil protection, and that's a matter to be determined in the course of the case. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish, I may be of assistance. Delic told you a few moments ago from 5 onwards is the task of the Pristina Corps. The previous paragraphs, he said where they come from, and that is going to be an answer to this question that you've been putting, how come that paragraph 2 is there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me ask you about another topic, the coordination with the MUP. In 1999, when you were tasked to carry out joint actions, how was that coordination done? You -- you explained to us that you got the order via courier at least some of the time. Did -- did the -- did your MUP counterpart receive the same order or a similar order through his -- through his organ and then did the two of you meet? How -- how did that work in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received orders down my own chain. I don't know what the chain is for the MUP to receive their orders, but usually I would speak to the chief of the secretariat, because the chief of the secretariat in the territory is the counterpart of the commander. They're in the same town. Usually he would have the same information that the -- the unit, the company of the PJP that is in that town, and one of the MUP detachments that is in that territory would take part. After all, that is what is written in my own order, what MUP units are going to be there. It was his duty to ensure -- because in my barracks, there weren't any facilities for us to meet, so usually we would meet at the MUP premises and then that is where we would carry out coordination. Coordination is reaching agreement and commanders of MUP units took part in this; also commanders of the local PJP companies; and the chief of the secretariat was just in attendance. After that, I would return to my unit. I would call my Chief of Staff, my operations officer, and I would draft documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you -- you had the -- the Joint Command order, which would be an order for routing and destroying the terrorists in a certain area. Did you see -- did -- did the police, did the MUP, have that same order? Did they have that same order and map like you did that described in general terms what the -- what the task was about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received orders for the same task; that is to say, that we received orders for the same task, but I received the orders I received, although "Joint Command" is written on them, but I got them from my command, from the command of the Pristina Corps; whereas, the MUP got their orders from some command of theirs in Pristina. I don't know what their name was, was it a MUP staff or something. However, when we were carrying out coordination, I would have my own order, and I don't know what kind of a document the MUP had. I always used my own order and my own part of the map, the one that I got from Pristina. I would use an ordinary pencil on my map, which was empty, and then I would mark some elements that I needed for coordination, and then later on I would transfer that to my officers so that they could carry out my order and draw a -- my decision. And as far as the map is concerned, sometimes -- sometimes that would be in the order of the corps command -- we would use a coded map, which was the same for the army and for the MUP. That is a map for maintaining communication. And even at corps command level there, is the same map with the same numbers that I -- like the one I have. And that is used for maintaining communication between and among different units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. You're saying that when you had a coded map, the MUP would have also had the same map with the same code markings on it? Right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what was written in some orders. This is a map on which there were only some numbers. It is only some numbers that were marked there. And with these numbers I wouldn't have to say I'm going to Pristina -- to Prizren, for instance. I would say I'm going to number 51. And the same map was in Pristina and I had the same map too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the MUP had the same map; right? Because you're working together and you have to understand when you're talking about a number, you have to be sure it means the same thing for both of you. Right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about meeting with the -- the PJP commander. Did you have any joint operations with -- that included either the -- the SAJ, the S-A-J, from the MUP or the JSO, during either 1998 or 1999? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, on one occasion I supported the SAJ. That was when Orahovac was being liberated. After that I was no longer with the SAJ. As for this other unit, I was never with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You never had any dealings with the JSO and only once with the SAJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once or perhaps twice we were neighbours, but the JSO, I just came across them en route once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the SAJ at that time you mentioned regarding Orahovac in 1998, how was that coordination done? Did you also -- did they sit in a meeting with you, as well as PJP, to do the coordination?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time was completely different. I was in the field when I got a call from the commander, General Pavkovic, and I already knew that Orahovac had been captured for one whole day. I was close to Rogovo with one of my combat groups. General Pavkovic told me that that afternoon MUP would move to liberate Orahovac and from that location where I was, I was supposed to support the MUP forces at his request. Since I said to him I had no communication with the MUP, no contact with them, no way to get in touch, he told me that they would be coming to Zrze, there would be a PJP unit from Djakovica, and later on SAJ would come. That's where I got in touch with them, and I was with them that first day. That was the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to the JSO, you said you came across them en route once or twice. Do you recall if that was in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 I only saw the members of that unit, a few of them. In 1998 I saw a few members of that unit in town, in Djakovica. As I was passing by, they were in the yard of the MUP secretariat in Djakovica. And in 1999 I saw -- it was sometime in the beginning of April, after our combat action was completed, I saw that unit or a part thereof. They had a few vehicles of their own and we ran into each other on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And what area was that when you came across them in 1999 in April?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. General, you were aware of the plan in 1998 called "Grom 98"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of something called Grom. I thought it had something to do with this five-stage plan. I am not able to tell you anything about that with any certainty. I heard of Grom, but what exactly that means, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was something to do with the five-stage plan, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know in -- in the Milosevic trial there was some evidence about Colonel Crosland and Paddy Ashdown being in Kosovo and reportedly seeing shelling in the area of Suva Reka and surrounding villages. I just want to ask you: When was that? Do you recall when they were there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is video footage. That was September 1998. But at the Milosevic trial I challenged --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I understand that --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that the Good Lord could have seen what he claims to have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just wanted to know when it was. Let me ask you one last area and then I'll -- I'll finish up, General. At -- on the 4th of December, on Tuesday this week, you -- you were answering a question about informing MUP. You said: "In a similar way, we would inform the MUP" -- this is at page 19456, line 2. "In a similar way, we would inform the MUP if we were to notice anything untoward happening on the territory which did not come under our competence and something that the MUP should see to and resolve or if there was something linked to the members of the police force generally speaking." And you were then asked: "And not only the police but civilians too?" And you said: "Yes." Now, if you saw crimes being committed by MUP members in 1999 during the war, what action would you take?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on specific circumstances. In any case, if there is the smallest chance for me to prevent the commission of a crime, I would certainly do that. The last resort would be that if I cannot prevent it, I would report it to their commanding officer, their chief, and demand that he take steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any MUP members committing crimes during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever -- did you ever have it reported to you by your subordinates or by civilians, by anyone, that MUP had committed crimes in -- in your area? Did that happen during the war in 1999 even once?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received notification from my subordinates, but not about crimes, about some other acts on several occasions, and I passed that on to my colleague in the MUP. Some observations of my commanding officers from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what kind of observations are you talking about? You say they were not crimes. What were the observations about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could treat it as a criminal offence. Inappropriate treatment of a civilian, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what we want to know about. What kinds of observations were you receiving from your subordinates about MUP engaging in inappropriate treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, eight years later you're asking me for details. I'm telling you in every specific case, if my commanding officer reported to me that somebody was mistreating a civilian, I would report it to my colleague -- or rather, inform him that in such-and-such a place his policemen are not working properly and that he should take steps because they were mistreating a specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall any specific examples of the mistreatment? Can you tell us something more specific? Are you talking about murder, rape, robbery, or just an insult?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way. No murders. I never heard of any rapes. As for theft or robbery, I believe that sort of thing happened, but I cannot give you the place now. Maybe it's written somewhere in one of my reports. But at any rate, I informed my colleague about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did you never report up to the Pristina Corps that MUP members were engaging in criminal activity against the civilian population during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, on one occasion, in one report, I know for sure that there is a reference to that. But it was not about civilian population. I believe theft or robbery is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Theft or robbery against whom? Civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were abandoned houses, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So what I would term "looting" by MUP members; is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to imply a multitude of occurrences. I said that I had written something like that in one of my reports to the superior command, but we cannot talk about a multitude of cases. It was an individual case, or maybe several cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you write that up? When did you send that report up to General Lazarevic or the Pristina Corps? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good morning. It's me again.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We owe the Trial Chamber one piece of information. Namely, on Tuesday - that's on page 19401 of the transcript - you responded to my question about the terrorist who was arrested in Prizren, and the Presiding Judge asked if we had any identification for that person. That's why I would like to call up Exhibit 5D228. General, you recognize this sort of document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at 1.2, the second item. It begins with the words, "Guards of the support battalion" -- "Guards of the logistical battalion," rather. Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Guards of the logistical battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade captured terrorist Gashi Shukri, son of Dervish, who was under --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you read more slowly. Just start again. We've lost the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Guards of the Logistics Battalion of the 549 Motorised Brigade took into custody terrorist Gashi Shukri, son of Dervish, who was moving under cover around the redeployment area of the unit. Before his capture, he discarded an AP rifle with three clips of ammunition and a knife marked 'KLA'." He confessed that he was a member of the terrorist organisation KLA. He's being processed by the security organs and the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to corroborate this, we also have an exhibit; namely, the criminal report against Gashi Shukri, which is 5D903.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, Prosecutor Hannis put to you a number of questions about volunteers. You answered that you had them in your unit. You stated that there were some foreign nationals as volunteers within your existing units. What I want to know is how they came to you, how they came to be included in your units.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came in an organised way. One of the centres for volunteers was in Belgrade. They rallied there. They were trained. They were subjected to medical examinations, after which they were sent to the admissions centre of the 3rd Army in Nis. As far as I know, they underwent training there from seven to ten days in duration, and then depending on the requirements of the Pristina Corps, they would be transferred to the Pristina Corps to specific brigades. And there they were assigned according to their military occupational specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you perhaps recall the legislation concerned? Was it allowed for foreign nationals to be members of the army during the war as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that matter is stipulated in the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army, I believe. I don't know the exact article.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens Exhibit number P984, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have the Law on the Army before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Could we have Article 8, please. The next page, please. I think that in English it is on the third -- third page. Could we zoom in Article 8, please. Also in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, look at Article 8, and could you please read aloud the third paragraph of that article, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Service in the army shall be performed only by Yugoslav citizens. As an exception - in time of war - also individuals who do not have Yugoslav citizenship may also serve if they join the army as volunteers."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Hannis put to you yesterday the two analyses you made, one for the action in Jeskovo, which is numbered 51998 [as interpreted], and the deblocking of Retimlje and the road to Orahovac, P1995. It says that there were no persons captured or arrested in those actions. The first exhibit was P1998. I would like to know whether anybody was arrested during your actions, your operations.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean earlier operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I mean any operations you performed.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of times, especially on the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the procedure of arrest?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When such persons are arrested, they are first disarmed, searched, then they are restrained, escorted, and within the shortest possible time they are turned over to security authorities to be identified, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you perhaps remember why in those two operations that I just mentioned nobody was arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to these two activities -- but we should make a distinction there, because as far as Jeskovo is concerned, I was directly there on the ground, and you can read in the security organ's report and in the book of that commander that was a special unit. For the duration of the fighting, we constantly heard those cries, "Allahu Akbar," they were all in black uniforms and none of them surrendered. None of them discarded their weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a special unit. Whose special unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A special unit of the KLA. Specifically of the 125th Brigade of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in this second operation nobody was arrested either. You mentioned something about columns of people, convoys.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that second activity, the terrorists persistently defended that area, Upper and Lower Retimlje, Randubrava, Studencane, and the route along which they were withdrawing together with the civilian population. It goes through Dobrodeljane towards Pagarusa. I knew that in this first sector the 124th Brigade is located. And I knew that the 123rd Brigade was somewhere to the north-west of Suva Reka. But in this territory, practically from Malisevo and Suva Reka, in that territory there were five terrorist brigades from the operations zone Pastrik, and they defended this route bitterly, persistently. In several places where my commanding officers showed me, I found blood-stains, soldiers' caps soaked with blood, pieces of a human skull in one place even, but not in a single place could you find a dead body of the terrorist, because they fought to the last until they had pulled their last man out. And only six terrorists in six -- in black uniforms, but that's a special unit of their General Staff where we had hand-to-hand combat, there were only those six we found dead, dressed as Mujahedin, in black uniforms and long beards. Those were the only six bodies we found on the ground. We can only assume for the rest how many casualties they had, and we found around 30 fresh graves in a place near Pagarusa and we supposed that that's where they buried their fallen fighting men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You won't be finishing during this period? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will finish in next 20 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Another break, Mr. Delic. Could you leave, please, with the usher, again. We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, I just wanted to introduce two new faces on our side over here. To my far right is Eleni Vossou, an intern who will be working with us. To my immediate right is a Vladimir Petrovic, who's an intern working with us as well, to be distinguished from Vladimir Petrovic on the other side. It's part of our effort to maintain equality of arms with the Defence. We've got equality of Petrovics. I don't know if we'll ever get a Mr. Fila on this side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just a few more questions. My colleague asked you about the area of responsibility of the brigade or the zone of responsibility. You marked it in blue on IC153. That was a map. You marked the sectors of deployment. But outside of the border belt and the area of deployment that you marked, were you responsible for public law and order and the security -- or safety of person and property of the citizens in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because during the war in my territory, in the Prizren sector, all the organs functioned normally; local self-government, the MUP, the judiciary, all the other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, in answer to a question by my colleague Mr. Lukic, you mentioned military check-points. I would now like to know the following: At the military check-points, were military personnel -- military police officers had powers vis-a-vis which persons?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, only persons in military uniforms. Only soldiers, reserve soldiers, volunteers, all those who wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question stems from that answer. Are you responsible in a state of war for the status of other structures in the defence system? So if there's another unit of the Army of Yugoslavia that has not been re-subordinated to you, MUP, civilian protection, civil defence, the municipal assembly, and so on?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am responsible for my units, the units that reinforced my units and the re-subordinated units. As for all the other units, I can be made responsible for them only in terms of logistics, supplies, or whatever is written in an order that has to be issued by my superior command to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to all those other structures that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as regards all the other structures, there can be cooperation with them, if necessary, because they're also state institutions, organs, and so on, so there can be exchange of information. In some cases when some of those civilian structures are involved, some assistance can be provided to them. But as a rule, everyone is supposed to do their own job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, was there a military administration, military rule?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need for that. I've already indicated that all the state organs functioned fully in my area, completely normally, despite the difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave us an answer regarding the check-points. Now I would like to move on to a different topic. My colleague Mr. Hannis asked you yesterday and today some questions about that, and this is the basis for my next question. During the war, did you, as a brigade commander, issue any tasks in any way whatsoever to any structures that involved armed population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my area, I never saw any non -- any armed non-Siptar population, because as early as in 1998 the people had already been expelled from all the villages in which they were in the majority. In my area, there was also the village of Novake and the village of Velika Hoca, where Serbs were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, to follow up on that and another question by Mr. Hannis, he showed you an order, and you can see here that there are no tasks for the civilian population. This concerns Jezerce. You explained that this term was used as the level of the municipality. What I would like to know is whether it would be necessary for an engagement of any such structures of the armed population - but let me extend that to include also the civil defence and the civilian protection - for a specific order on the re-subordination to be issued by their organ in charge? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had any such decision been made or such an order been issued, on the re-subordination, for instance of a ministry detachment with all the units -- ministry department with all the units that are linked with it, then the situation would be different. I would have had the right to set tasks to them. But as -- as it was, they worked in accordance with their own plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In item 2 of the order we saw that mention was made of the armed non-Siptar population. That was Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P1978 [as interpreted], order of the Joint Command for the Jezerce action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was translated as P1978. I think it's P1976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in item 2, you explained this reference to the armed non-Siptar population. What I'm interested in is whether such a provision in an order comes from a higher level or is it the product of the work of the level -- of this particular level?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, item 2 in every order comes from the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague Mr. Hannis asked you about the term "singleness of command" or "unity of command." We saw in your analysis post-action reports. You explained -- or rather, you explained that there was combined command over the military and MUP forces, and you stressed that there were two separate chains of command that remained intact, the MUP chain of command and the Army of Yugoslavia chain of command. Now, I would like to explore the difference between those two terms, "objedinjena," combined command, and "jedinstvena komanda," unified command.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unified command would imply that there is a single chain of command. And when you have combined command, I don't know how it worked with other commanders, but in my case that's how I worked with this MUP unit right from the start. I came to realize that the easiest thing would be for me and the MUP unit commander to meet in a certain place. He would come accompanied with some of his organs; I would come accompanied with some of my own organs. And everybody commanded their own units. And if any actual concerted -- concerted or coordinated action was required, then there would be no middleman. The two of us would deal with it directly. He would ask for help or support from me directly, and I would provide it by deploying the required unit. So no time was lost. It was very efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
