utterances.text: Para 3.1 says that Combat Group 1 of the 15th Armoured Brigade, on the morning of 19 December, 1998, deployed in the area of Batlavsko Lake for regular company exercises. While doing so, they were observed and filmed by the OSCE mission members. The usual practice was for OSCE mission members to escort convoys of the Army of Yugoslavia to their point of destination, but it says here that filming was not allowed for the simple reason that it was not possible to film this very narrow area of Batlava Lake, when the exercises were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood well, it was always a training ground of the army.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform the security administration of the General Staff this telegram reached them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I said that every day in the course of 1998, until March 1999, I sent daily telegrams to the security section of the 3rd Army and the security administration of the General Staff of VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did any members of the OSCE mission give you any information? And while you give us an answer, let us look at 5D1309, paras 2.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a reference to a diplomat here. He's named. And this diplomat provided some information. Maybe we should go into private session? Or can we just show it this way openly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll show it without exposing it to the public. And there's no need for you to refer to the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please don't read the name aloud. Just give us your comments. What kind of information did you receive from one of the diplomats? It's 5D1309, penultimate paragraph, 2.6?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As part of our regular exchange with the state security sector for Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupt you. It's page 2 in English. The Trial Chamber needs to follow as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The military security service also had a regular exchange with the State Security Service, and this paragraph contains intelligence available to the State Security Service about the contacts that one member of the verification mission had -- sorry, it's, rather, a comment that many reports of the OSCE mission about the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija are objective, but two out of three top men in the KVM select among this information and channel it further on towards -- that is, depending on the national interests of their respective countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, at that time, in December, in addition to this information about continued activity on the part of the terrorists, in terms of training and arming, already then, in December, in addition to the presence of the OSCE mission, did you have intelligence to the effect the Albanians were leaving the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There was quite a bit of knowledge to that effect. First of all, the leaders of the terrorist units of the KLA were sending their -- their families away throughout 1998 -- or rather, in the second half of 1998. They primarily moved them to the territory of the Republic of Macedonia and the Republic of Albania. Also, we learned through electronic surveillance --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, but while you are talking, let's have a look at 3D1034. It is yet another one of your telegrams, dated the 22nd of December, I think. And could you give us your comments on point 2.2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I started talking about. 2.2 has to do with the results of measures of electronic surveillance whereby information was received indicating increased belligerence among KLA members and a desire for revenge because of the recent deaths of some of their members during an all-out action to stop the entry of terrorists in the area of the Liken border post when 36 terrorists were liquidated. In all of these localities that were under the control of the terrorists, there was a curfew from 10.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m., and then the Siptars, rather than do anything else, moved their families through illegal channels and sent them abroad. The information that we received from telephone communications indicated that Albanians from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were talking to their relatives, who were temporarily employed in European Union countries, and they were telling them to temporarily move from Kosovo, because in 1998 and 1999 that was the most undesirable of places in which one could live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we briefly look at 3.3 on the next page, because these villages are included in the indictment. So could you briefly tell us about your knowledge regarding 3.3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This has to do with the same incident. Our intelligence indicated that there were some wounded terrorists in the area of the Liken border post, which I talked about a few moments ago; that they were receiving medical treatment in villages like Celina in the Orahovac municipality. Also, this shows that the terrorists were planning yet again to attack some of our combat groups. Specifically here, Combat Group 3 of the 559th in the area of the village of Damjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And where was there a terrorist staff exactly? In what village? Is it correct that the terrorist staff was in the village of Velika Krusa?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had intelligence about strong terrorist -- strongholds in the villages of Velika Krusa, Bela Crkva, Kusljin, Drenovac. All of these are villages between Prizren and Djakovica. But the terrorist staffs were farther away from the roads, because the village of Velika Krusa is on the road between Prizren and Djakovica. The terrorists avoided placing their terrorist staffs and headquarters close to important roads. They preferred inaccessible terrains, but they did send some of their groups out into roads, organising ambushes, and our forces sustained casualties on a daily basis due to these ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to show you a document now of the 3rd Army dated the 5th of March of the security department from the 5th of March, and could you please give us your comments on 2.2. Are you aware of what happened, and was that based on your intelligence? It is the 5th of March, 1999. 3D1050.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the paragraph that you'd like me to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This paragraph in this document states that "The Main Staff of the KLA for the Drenica sector, under the command of Sami Ljustaku, issued an order to evacuate the local civilian population" -- and I wish to note that in that area, the population is exclusively Albanian. So this civilian population is supposed to -- or rather, civilians from the villages at the foot of Mount Cicavica from the village of Drvare onwards to Vucitrn and station them in the depth of the territory of the Drenica sector. This also indicates forceful relocation of the population from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have two more documents. We'll have a look at them, and then we're not going to be dealing with documents any longer. I would be interested in the following: Your security service of the Pristina Corps, did it have any information indicating that the OSCE mission in Kosovo and Metohija went beyond the mandate entrusted to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Not the mission on the whole, but individual representatives of the OSCE mission. There is a great deal of information to that effect. Time permitting, I can give you a few examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a few.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The organs of the military security service arrested, documented, cut off, and then brought criminal charges in view of the intelligence activity of Kastrati, Bekim who was a lieutenant -- or rather, a member of the Army of Yugoslavia previously. During these proceedings, he confessed that when the mission of the OSCE arrived in Kosovo and Metohija from two members of the OSCE mission who were US citizens he was recruited by them and he was in this way recruited by the intelligence services of the United States of America. He also confessed that these same members of the OSCE mission recruited three other fellow citizens of his, and it was their task to observe the locations, positions, strength and activities of the army and MUP forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and to inform the two mentioned OSCE mission members via telephone using numbers that they had left them. When the OSCE mission withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, Bekim Kastrati was equipped with a satellite telephone by these two OSCE mission members in order to continue communicating with the OSCE mission, which withdrew into the Republic of Macedonia, and -- as is well known, and in the beginning of the war he provided information to these two members of the mission about the activities, positions, strength, and composition of MUP and army units in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Kastrati was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That will do, General.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I just say a few more things?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at this one example that we have in written form too. And could you give us your comments on that. 5D1311. Our time is limited. Since this is a multiple-page document. This is the command of the 3rd Army, the security department. I think that they sent this to the Supreme Command Staff. And on page 1, there is a letter stating that two statements of the KLA -- of members of the KLA are attached to this document. And on the next page, we see a statement of Aslan Sopi. That is page 6, in e-court; in B/C/S, in page 4. So could you please give us your comments with regard to the end of the second paragraph. So it's page 6 in e-court -- I meant English. And in B/C/S, it is page 4. Yes. I see.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, the second paragraph. "In addition to these forms of assistance ..." It's a long paragraph. Can you see where it says "in addition to these types of assistance"? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. "In addition to these forms of assistance" -- well, Mr. Aslan Sopi, who was arrested, states here in his statement that the terrorist staffs are receiving assistance through various humanitarian organisations. However, I believe it is particularly important to point out that he says that the territory -- that the terrorist staff in the Llab region that was commanded by a commander whose nickname was Remi was regularly visited by terrorists, and then he describes how old they were and what they looked like. Every day they came in, as he says here, even twice a day. And they gave them information about them bringing maps, military maps, that included the disposition of units of the VJ and the MUP in the territory of all of Kosovo and Metohija. So these three members of the OSCE provided coded maps to the KLA terrorists where the positions of the MUP and army units in Kosovo were marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 101, line 22, it says "was regularly visited by terrorists," where in fact the witness said by the -- the three members of the OSCE mission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to move on faster, 5D1310 is within the same context, but we are going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have just spoken about these maps, that you had information from the terrorists about these maps. Could we have a look at 5D1312 now. This seems to be information from the Supreme Command Staff, and enclosed are some maps where the positions of the army are marked. And it seems of civilians and the KLA. Could you give us your comments and tell you whether you know about this -- tell us whether you know about this. So this first page is information from the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. May I correct you? It is from the intelligence administration of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is this information that they received from you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is information that they received through their own activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you now please take a look -- or rather, this refers to precisely marked positions and coordinates of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP. And could we please have a look at the last page. Can you give us your comments and tell us whether this is a coded map and what is marked there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On my screen, the map is not positioned properly. Now it's all right. This is a coded map that the terrorist staffs from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija submitted to the representatives of the NATO representatives in Macedonia, and in it the positions of civilians and KLA members are marked, and I assume that these arrows -- rather, it includes the positions of the army as well, and the arrows indicate the planned activity of the army. The aim of this report is to inform NATO where civilians are so that they would not bomb civilians. And here you see the KLA as well, which is to say the KLA positions are marked there too. So in fact, this was a handover of information on the location of military units and also the location of civilians and of the KLA. So that is useful for later planning of bombing specific targets in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did this come into the hands of the intelligence administration of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the intelligence administration has a series of measures -- or rather, a methodology of work which is rather similar to the work of the military security service. However, the volume of work is different. Through their operative positions in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, they got ahold of such maps and they informed the Supreme Command Staff about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- that really doesn't help. Was someone arrested? Was there a -- a mole who handed it over? How -- how did it come into the hands of the intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one of the methods of work - and I think that this document says so, as well; I'll try to find the passage - well, they received this through their contacts and their positions in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the intelligence administration did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- so one side are trying to pass information to NATO, and someone else is undermining the efforts to pass information to NATO; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, precisely. Your Honour, there were many loyal Albanians in the area of Kosovo and Metohija who were not extremists and who were not terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to other activities of your agency. After the OSCE mission left Kosovo and Metohija and after the NATO air-strikes began, what kind of security problems did you face then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the OSCE mission left and the air-strikes began -- if you mean the military security service, I can say we faced a multitude of problems. The greatest problems were primarily security problems and very difficult conditions of work under day and night bombing. And a particular security problem was the beginning of massive migration of population out of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said the problem of migration of the Albanian population, but we don't have it in the transcript. Never mind. You say "problem."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why was it a problem? Why was it a problem to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a multifaceted problem when the Army of Yugoslavia did not believe it was natural and desirable. We were rather surprised by the fact that a certain number of Albanians are beginning to move out in an organised way. We, in the command of the Pristina Corps, were very much concerned over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the reasons ethnic Albanians were leaving Kosovo and Metohija, and did you know whether Serbs were leaving as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I said a moment ago that the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was the last place on earth where normal life could go on, so people were going away, fearing for their own safety. That's one reason. And the second reason is that a lot of misinformation was being spread by a certain number of ethnic Albanians, dissemination of leaflets by night into people's mailboxes, and these leaflets said that the right moment is being awaited for armed struggle and that Podujevo is especially in danger because it's on the border with Serbia; that Chetniks would come from Serbia and slit all of their throats. So fearing for their own security and because of that misinformation and various rumours, people started to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As a soldier who graduated from the highest military schools, can you give us your assessment. Was it -- was it a good thing for the army that people were leaving, from the viewpoint of war, the air-strikes, the expected -- the anticipated ground invasion? Or ground aggression?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyone with a modicum knowledge of military matters would know and tell you that this massive evacuation of the Albanian population was not a good thing for the Army of Yugoslavia. It weakened the army directly for a very simple reason: We in the corps command knew very well that our forces in Kosovo and Metohija were safe as long as the population was there. If the population moved out, then NATO pilots would have an easy job of bombing. They would no longer have to worry about choosing their targets. So we, in the army, did not want the population to move out. We felt safer as long as people were still living in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you just please slow down for the interpretation. My next question is: As a member of the collegium of the command of the Pristina Corps, did you hear at any time, at collegium meetings or any other meetings in the corps command, of the existence of a plan or any measures or procedures geared at driving out Albanian civilians from the province?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not as a member of the collegium of the corps, not as a member of the security organs of the Pristina Corps have I ever encountered a piece of intelligence or any other information that would indicate that somebody was ordering or planning or carrying out this massive expulsion of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you try to use the media to appeal to the ethnic Albanian population not to move out, to warn them, to explain?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you just one example. Albanian news -- Albanian language newspapers Bujko and Koha Ditore in Kosovo and Metohija, for instance, refused to publish such an appeal by the government of Serbia, an appeal to Albanian people not to move out and to stay in their homes. I personally believe that it was part of a preconceived plan and scenario to use this evacuation, this migration as a way to present it all as a major humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain how the command of the Pristina Corps operated after the beginning of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the Pristina Corps - which before the NATO aggression held regular meetings of its collegium on a daily basis; those were regular meetings and extended meetings, that is, those attended by commanders of subordinate units, such as brigades, were held once a week - changed its method of work. Just before the NATO aggression started, the command of the Pristina Corps abandoned its peacetime location and did not return until the day the army withdrew completely from Kosovo. And after moving from that location, they deployed dispersively in various locations around Pristina and changed these locations frequently. As for the meetings of the collegium, they were no longer held in full composition. Instead, the head of the collegium held one-on-one meetings with a narrow circle of members, for safety reasons among other things, because there was bombing day and night, but throughout the command functioned continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At those meetings, in addition to the corps command members, were other people present, such as representatives of the local self-government, party personnel, persons, and other politicians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I claim categorically that no, that was not the case. The meetings of the Pristina Corps command were attended only by the officers from the Pristina Corps or, at times, the 3rd Army commander, or some other officers from the 3rd Army command, depending on the nature of the problems discussed at the collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And before NATO air-strikes began?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This also applies to the period before the NATO air-strikes began.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What issues within your remit did you report on to the corps commander at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I, as the chief of the security organ, informed the commander regularly about all the security phenomena in the units and the security phenomena that affected the security of the units, facilities, and commands, the facilities that were protected by the military security service. I also informed the commander about the strength, the location, the plans, the intentions, the arming process, and the activities of the Albanian terrorists. I also informed him about all the intelligence that was interesting from the security point of view from the Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in light of your personal experience and the experience from the reports of the subordinate security organs, did the commanders in practice take into account the assessments of the security organs and the orders of the -- of officers regarding sanctions to be applied against soldiers who committed disciplinary infractions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were all commanders that were highly responsible and professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the corps command take appropriate measures against those commanders who did not comply with the orders and the commanders in whose units there were omissions that had certain consequences?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. This was -- this kind of responsibility was at the very core of the operation of the Pristina Corps. The corps commander regularly, as regards the commanders of those units that did not comply with the orders and did not take into account the observations of the security organs and who would not comply with the orders and that resulted in certain consequences, he would take certain measures, either in terms of personnel policy, disciplinary, or even criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think that must in English be as regards the members of those units. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you said "criminal prosecution." Could the corps commander take such measures?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the corps commander can institute criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but through whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, through the competent organs of the security service and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does he have the powers to impose criminal sanctions on anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the corps commander does not have the power to impose criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, now that you're talking about those omissions in certain units and the possibility for the commander to take certain measures, in terms of personnel policy, could you please tell us some -- give us some examples of some measures that were taken by the commander during the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a number of such measures. As far as I can remember at this time, for instance, the commander of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade, Colonel Milentijevic, was removed from his post and criminal proceedings were instituted against him. Then the commander of the 175 Infantry Brigade, Colonel Petrovic was also removed from his post. Several battalion commanders. I think about 40 battalion commanders were relieved of their duty, and some of the officers were brought before the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- that -- I'm sorry, Mr. Bakrac, but I think my intervention in relation to page 109, line 17 is inaccurate. This is all about action taken against commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I understood that you asked about the situation in the units, and that's why I said "yes." I didn't understand that you were asking me specifically who this referred to, the commanders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commanders and leaders. Komandanti and komandiri, depending on the level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over what period do you say 40 commanders were relieved of their duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40 battalion commanders were removed from the post, most of them before the beginning of the NATO aggression. I can't recall the exact figure, but that was before the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, during what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the period between March and June, the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to note that on page 111, line 13, the witness said, "Most of them after the beginning of the NATO aggression."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the transcript reflects a different answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And one of them was prosecuted. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several of them were prosecuted, had criminal charges brought against them. But I am talking about brigade commanders here. I'm talking about the highest level of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you're talking about battalion commanders. It's been translated in English as "brigade." Have I got that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it's a bit confusing, because what he said was: "One commander of the 58th light Infantry Brigade, Milentijevic, was sent to a military court to be court-martialled, and the 175th units commander was replaced and then he talks about 40-something other officers. He makes a distinction between two types of commander, as in komandir and komandant. In English, there is no such distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you intending to explore what the criminal charges were? Because if not, I would like to ask what were the criminal charges brought against commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you recall what was the indictment against Milentijevic, the commander of the 58th Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 58th Brigade is a brigade that is fully replenished from the reserve force. Lieutenant Colonel Milentijevic was replaced for the following reason: Certain military conscripts from his units demonstrated a lack of discipline. In this specific case, it had to do with the following: A group of military conscripts took a vehicle and went to their respective homes. The vehicle had an extent and some of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Stojanovic, you were asked what was the criminal -- or what were the criminal charges against the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the commander here, Lieutenant-Colonel Milentijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What were the criminal -- you said that he was the subject of criminal charges. What were these criminal charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For failure to take action to protect the health and lives of persons which resulted in the death of certain members of his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you -- you were also translated into English as saying -- you were talking about brigade commanders here. I'm talking about the highest level of command. Now, the one you've just dealt with was a brigade commander, but have you mentioned any other brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I mentioned the commander of the 175th Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was his --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the charges against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was replaced because by failing to take necessary measures, he made it possible for a group of volunteers from his unit to commit crimes in the village of Zegra, we later prosecuted that. And that is why he was replaced from his duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is Colonel Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are there any other either brigade or battalion commanders that were the subject of prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commanders of brigades, Mr. President? I don't have information about others. As for lower levels of command, like battalion commanders and company commanders, there were several of them. There is Captain Petrovic, who had criminal charges brought against him and who was actually convicted. I think from the 202nd Logistics Base. But that does exist in the documents of the relevant military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have these documents here, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with this witness, no. But we will have representatives. We'll have a judge and a prosecutor from the military court as witnesses here, and we are going to tender documents through them on the cases that were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to deal with before we interrupt for the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I would like to move on to another topic, so yes, well, there is one minute left, but this may be a good point to take a break -- or rather, to finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you could perhaps think overnight of -- of more details of these officers who were in command of units at battalion level who you know were the subject of criminal proceedings, and you can tell us more about that tomorrow morning. We have to bring our proceedings today to an end. We will resume at 9.00 o'clock --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom. Meanwhile, overnight it's vital that you should have no discussion whatsoever with any person about the evidence in this case. And that means any of the evidence, whether it's given by you or by anyone else, any discussions you have between now and returning here should be about other subjects. Discussion of the evidence is off limits. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there's something you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a matter relating to an order made on the 5th of October by this Court that the Defence for General Lukic submit the father's name and other particulars in respect to persons on the witness list by the 30th of November, a date which has passed, and the order has not been complied with. I don't think it is something the Prosecution needs to file anything about, but I think we should place on record that the fact that the Defence has failed to comply with the order so far is hugely inconvenient, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, can you assist on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. I just learned from my assistant that Mr. Ivetic is working on that issue as well, apart from the translation issue. And I have one -- one more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- with your leave. We called the Detention Unit and asked them if it's possible to visit Mr. Lukic on Saturday, because we have only next week before we depart from our respective homes, and I need one full day to discuss our future witnesses with Mr. Lukic. And with this schedule, it's not possible. So if you can assist us with the prison warden to allow us, me and Mr. Ivetic, to visit our client on Saturday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The whole day would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll investigate that and let you know what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
